newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: COLSTON'S RESPONSE EXPECTED BY SENATE PRESIDENT NEXT WEEK
Senate President, Margaret Reid, says she's received a message that her deputy, Senator Mal Colston will contact her next week.
The government, opposition, minor parties and fellow independent, Brian Harradine, have all called on Senator Colston to stand down as Deputy Senate President.
Senator Reid echoed that call .. and has tried twice to contact Senator Colston, who was discharged from a Brisbane private hospital yesterday.

Senator Reid, who was advised Senator Colston would contact her when he was out of hospital, says she received a message this morning, through Senator Colston's electorate office, to say he's still convalescing and will make contact next week.
OPPOSITION SAYS CALLS COULD RISE
The Federal Opposition claims the cost of phone calls could rise as a result of Telstra having to pay a one-off three-billion dollar dividend to the Federal Government.
Telstra's board has approved the special payment, which will have to be funded by new borrowings, a move that's resulted in a downgrading of Telstra's domestic credit rating.
The Government insists Telstra will continue to have a strong balance sheet despite being placed further into debt by the three billion dollar loan.
Labor's Communication spokesman, Chris Schacht, says Telstra will clearly need to increase call charges or impose fees on directory assistance calls to pay the interest on the new borrowings.
Senator Schacht says forcing the extra debt onto Telstra makes the Government's criticism at the last election about Australia's debt levels hypocritical in the extreme.
PARTNER OF WOMAN LAUNCHES BROADSIDE AT ANDREWS

The partner of a woman who's died after being denied use of the Northern Territory's voluntary euthanasia law, has described Federal politician Kevin Andrews as misguided, evil, and wicked. Fifty-six-year-old Esther Wild died yesterday of a rare form of stomach cancer.
She had qualified to use the Territory's Right To Die law, but was prevented by a successful private members bill put forward by Mr Andrews.
Ms Wild's partner Martin Williams told ABC Television, Mr Andrews is riding around in the name of Christianity of which he has no concept.
MCCAFFERTY TO BE RELEASED
Convicted murder Archie McCafferty will be released from his New South Wales prison after being granted parole in Sydney today.
The Federal Government plans to send McCafferty back to his native Scotland, despite the killer's wish that he remain in Australia.
Mr McCafferty's lawyer says he'll appeal any attempt to deport his client.
HOTEL REFUTES CENSORSHIP CLAIM
A Perth hotel which has cancelled the booking for a breakfast function featuring Independent MP Pauline Hanson, says the cancellation has nothing to do with Ms Hanson's attendance.
West Australian Independent, Paul Filing, has accused Burswood Resort of censorship by cancelling the booking.
Burswood's Public Relations Manager, Bruce Brislin, says the booking was cancelled because major renovations had been scheduled for the venue.
He says the booking was only tentative, and says Mr Filing was informed the venue was unavailable within two days.

Mr Brislin says while the attendance of Pauline Hanson had nothing to do with the cancellation, the Hotel has the right to refuse any business that may cause some disruption to normal operational activities.
CRACK-DOWN ON ILLEGAL ALIENS
The Federal Government is cracking down on illegal entrants and people who overstay their visas.
The government's increasing the number of agencies which exchange data to help find people who unlawfully receive medicare or welfare payments.
The Tax Office and Immigration and Social Security departments already exchange information, and Medicare will soon join the network.
Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock says new figures show there are more than 45-thousand people who are in Australia illegally - costing taxpayers millions of dollars a year in unlawful payments.
Mr Ruddock says it's no longer a case of whether these people are caught, but when.
